pages.text:
6:47.

The roar hit me, but it didn't stick. The ceiling was the same, and the light was the same, but then I saw the sun coming through the window at a higher, softer angle. Gus was not screaming into my face. He was whispering.

"Max! It's Sunday! The truck's here!"

I sat up, and my brain felt like static on an old radio. I let out a short, surprised bark of a laugh, and then I realized my eyes were wet. I wiped them with my sleeve, pretending it was just dust from the boxes.

There was a knock at the door. Mom’s voice came through, bright and crisp. "Page six, item one. Up and at 'em."

I swung my legs off the bed, and the floor was cool under my socks. In the kitchen, Dad was fanning the toaster again, with smoke curling up thick and grey. He looked at me, hopeful, holding a slice of charcoal.

"Anti-gravity," he said.

I grabbed the peanut butter. "Impossible to put down," I said.

He blinked, and then he grinned, wide and slow. "You caught me, Max. You caught me."

It was the best toast I had ever eaten.
pages.image: Max in a red hoodie sits at a table eating black toast with peanut butter, smiling; Dad in a fish apron stands by the toaster fanning smoke, looking surprised and happy; morning light streams through the window.

pages.text:
The moving truck sat in the driveway, blocking the sun with its white side. Two guys in blue shirts hauled boxes, their arms flexing under the weight of my old life. I stood on the porch, watching them, feeling like a spectator at a game I had already lost.

Mrs. Abernathy was on her porch across the street, wearing her floral gardening hat. She waved, small and steady, so I walked over to her before I got in the truck.

"It's a hot dish," I said, "so be careful, you'll want a trivet."

She burst out laughing, her whole body shaking. "Oh, Max! You are a menace. I will send one to Arizona. I promise." She hugged me, smelling like tomato vines and soap.

I walked back. Mr. Grady’s sprinkler was on, a high arc of water that soaked the mailman, who was hopping around in a puddle. I waved at him. He didn’t wave back, but he didn’t curse at me either.

The guys loaded the last box. I looked at the house. The yellow paint, the creaking porch, the spot on the lawn where the sprinkler had worn a bald patch. It looked smaller than it did from the inside.

I climbed into the truck. The seats were stiff and smelled like cardboard. I didn’t look back. I didn’t have to.
pages.image: Max on the porch waves to a tiny woman in a floral hat on the opposite porch; a sprinkler sprays water in an arc, soaking a mailman in a puddle; a large moving truck is visible in the background.

pages.text:
A shadow stretched across the truck's hood.

Jonah stood there, chest heaving. Sweat darkened his buzz cut, and his bike helmet stayed strapped on. He held out a small laminated card.

I took it. In careful marker, it read: SATURDAYS 6:47.

He didn't say goodbye. He just looked at me with those big, serious eyes. I reached into my pocket and pulled out the spare spiky T. rex tail I had kept in my hoodie. I handed it to him.

He looked at it. He looked at me. Then he tucked it into his pocket, right next to his walkie-talkie.

"See you Saturday," he said.

"See you Saturday," I replied.

He turned and ran down the street, his helmet bobbing. I watched him until he disappeared around the corner. The truck engine rumbled to life. The doors closed. The world outside became a blur of yellow house and green grass.

I held the card in my hand. The plastic was smooth and cool. It felt heavy, like a promise.
pages.image: Max in a truck holds a small laminated card; outside the window, a boy in a bike helmet runs away down a grassy street; the boy holds a green spiky toy tail.

pages.text:
1,700 miles stretched out ahead of us.

Gus was in the back seat, roaring at every state line. Every time we crossed one, he shouted, "DINOSAURS!" and pointed out the window at the passing trees and fields like he was naming them.

Tessa sat next to me. Her headphones were around her neck. She tapped her fingers on her knee, a quiet, steady beat that sounded exactly like the drum practice pad she was leaving behind. After a while, she reached over and took my hand. Her fingers were cold, but I held on tight.

Dad was driving. He was humming a song I didn’t know. Grandma Bea’s Buick was in the rearview mirror, following us. Her horn played a little tune, a bumpy, cheerful melody, until she turned off at the exit and vanished into the heat.

"Max," Dad said, "did you know that cactus is just a word for a plant that has given up on being polite?"

I laughed. It was a real laugh, the kind that comes from your belly and not your mouth.

"Bad pun," I said.

"Good pun," Dad said. "We're almost there."

The landscape changed. The green turned to brown, then to tan. The air outside the window looked dry and sharp, like a pencil point.
pages.image: Max and Tessa sit in the back seat of a car, holding hands; Gus in a T. rex costume points out the window; Dad drives with a mustache; the landscape outside is dry and brown.

pages.text:
The house in Tucson was tan and flat and shaped like a shoebox somebody had left out in the sun. We unloaded until it got dark. My new room had a window that faced a cactus, and the cactus, I have to report, faced right back.

Before bed I carried the clock into the front hall and hung it on the first hook I could find. At 11:59 the little door popped open. "Cuck-oo." One crooked, fussy note, and that was all. No swirling, no roaring, no 6:47. Just a bird made of wood, doing its job.

"Hey, Gerald," I said. "Thanks."

Here is what I know now, and then I'll leave you alone. Happiness isn't what happens when the day goes right. It's what you bring to the day, on purpose, before it has a chance to prove you wrong. It took me a hundred Saturdays to find that out. You can have it in one.

On Saturday I woke up at 6:46 with Waffles on my feet and a roar on the way. The walkie-talkie sat on my shelf, with a range of two miles and a whole desert of distance between us, completely useless. I wouldn't have traded it for anything.

At 6:47 my phone buzzed. It was Jonah, in his bike helmet, grinning.

"Is it Saturday?" he said.

"It's Saturday," I said, and I smiled before I even knew why, on purpose.
pages.image: Max stands in an empty tan hallway, looking at a small cuckoo clock on a hook; his family is visible in the background, unpacking boxes; warm afternoon light fills the room.
